title: Trump Threatens EU With 'Very Heavy Tariffs' Over Canada Associate Membership
excerpt: Hours after Ursula von der Leyen proposed making Canada the EU's first associate member, Trump called it "laughable" and warned of tariffs — unless Europe's intentions are "good."
body:
• President Trump warned the EU he could impose "very heavy tariffs" or "stop trading" if Canada becomes an EU associate member with what he deems "bad intention."
  • EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed Wednesday in Strasbourg that Canada become the bloc's first-ever associate member, with PM Mark Carney in attendance.
  • Von der Leyen stressed the move was "not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength"; France's EU minister said Washington has no veto over Europe's geopolitical choices.
  • The clash lands amid a US-Canada trade war, with Trump calling Canada a "terrible trade partner" and signing orders restricting US government purchases of Canadian goods.

President Donald Trump on Wednesday threatened the European Union with "very heavy tariffs" if it moves forward with a plan to make Canada the bloc's first associate member — a proposal floated hours earlier by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in her annual State of the Union address.

Speaking to reporters en route to an event in North Carolina, Trump called the idea "laughable." But he made the threat conditional: "If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," he said. "If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe."

Von der Leyen's overture

Von der Leyen announced the proposal in Strasbourg on Wednesday, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in attendance, as she sought to deepen ties among allies in what she called "an openly hostile world." She proposed opening the door for Canada to be the EU's first associate member, building on the existing EU-Canada free trade agreement CETA with a broader "Alliance for the Future" aimed at creating "a common prosperity and economic security space."

"In short, we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible," she said, adding that the partnership was "not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength."

"It is not up to the United States — or anyone else — to choose the political and geopolitical direction of the Europeans."

— Benjamin Haddad, France's European Minister

Ottawa's pivot

Canada has been actively courting Europe as its relationship with Washington deteriorates. The US and Canada nearly reached a trade agreement in late August, but talks collapsed at the last minute. Trump has signed orders banning the import of many Canadian dairy products, alcoholic beverages and motorcycles, retaliated for Canadian tariffs, and this week signed an order restricting US government purchases of Canadian goods. Canada is seeking to reduce its dependence on the United States, the destination for roughly 70% of its exports, and Carney has called for a "unique alliance" with the EU.

Impact & Analysis

The EU has historically resisted flexible alliances with no legal status, so associate membership for Canada would be genuinely unprecedented. With US-Canada tensions running hot — Trump has repeatedly floated making Canada the 51st US state, an idea Carney firmly rejects — Ottawa's European pivot is now a live fault line in Western trade policy. The EU itself has been on the receiving end of Trump's tariffs on allies over the past year, so fresh threats land on already strained relations.

Diaspora Angle

Canada hosts one of the world's largest Indian diasporas, and a deeper EU-Canada economic corridor could open new trade, mobility and student pathways — while fresh US tariff escalation would ripple through the global supply chains Indian exporters and NRIs rely on.

What's Next

Europe has not backed down: France's European minister said publicly the US has no power to veto the EU's geopolitical choices. Carney is due to address the European Parliament on Thursday — watch whether he turns von der Leyen's proposal into a formal negotiating track.
